title: Discussing Digital Art in 1Q 2025
body:
Peter Bauman: Hello everyone and welcome to this Le Random podcast. It's our second as a team of 2025. I'm your host, Peter Bauman, the Editor-in-Chief at Le Random. And today I'm joined by thefunnyguys, the co-founder and CEO of Le Random, and Conrad House, the Collection Lead. Today we're looking back at the first quarter of 2025. We're going to look at the big picture takeaways from the quarter, what some of our favorite artists and exhibitions were and basically what we enjoyed, but also what we noticed and what might need some more investigation from the quarter. It's a really interesting chat. We're really excited to share it. Let's begin.

Let's start with the first issue that we're going to discuss today. It's something that I think has been growing and getting louder in this first quarter of 2025. It's always been present, but the noise is getting louder. It's these visceral fears in this growing issue of ethics and AI. It's largely a response from artists, or at least framed on behalf of artists. It doesn't always seem to include the artists that are benefiting from the technology. At worst, the way it's presented is that generative AI is just insta-plagiarism. You press a button and out comes stolen copyrighted content. At best, some superficially appealing slop. It's really quick to dismiss when it's reduced to those terms.

Obviously there are some good points that they raise. Generative AI does rely on copyrighted material, pirated content in some circumstances. That's been proven. There are issues with scraping and artist consent, not only from images but from a tech standpoint. And there's a lot of legal gray areas that are being tested by these big companies. They're pushing these limits of these legal gray areas and it's being determined whether or not they've breached those limits from a legal perspective.

What's most worrying is that the ultimate winner seems to be Silicon Valley and these big tech companies like OpenAI. They're the winner when they're just extracting all of this data and content and talent from artists. It doesn't seem fair superficially, right? They also just say that things like fair use is essentially stealing. Their argument goes that it's so morally tainted that it shouldn't even be touched. Their argument mixes a lot of moral absolutism, a lot of loaded language. Again, they call it just this insta-plagiarism machine and it removes a lot of the nuance from the discussion.

Then there's also this conflation of legal and ethical claims. That's when they make a jump between something that they find maybe morally unpleasant. They equate that with something with legal certainty. What we do know, if anything, in regards to legality, is that there's only uncertainty, in that we don't know whether or not things like fair use can be constituted as theft at this point.

There's also just the generalization of the tech industry motives. Silicon Valley is this monolith, this extractive monolith. But what this does is ignore a lot of the history of the development of generative AI and these deep generative models that goes back to Canada and Montreal and Toronto and NYU. So there's this rich academic and foundational history with Hinton and LeCun, where all these big breakthroughs came, especially in deep generative learning in the last 20 years. They came far from Silicon Valley.

So the main point is that once you take care to start understanding the tech in a more deep way, some of the main arguments that they have, the transformative argument, when you're talking about n-degree latent space, it's almost impossible to really understand the degree to which a lot of this is transformed and it isn't just direct plagiarism. So, yeah, there's a lot of gray area. There's a lot of room for discussion and that's exactly what I want to hear from you guys. So what do you guys think about the louder and louder voicing of moral concerns and AI in this first quarter?

Conrad House: I think you hit it pretty on the dot, Peter, but it's something that's super complex. It's something that's super nuanced. And it's more than ever something that's more gray area than anything else, and specifically the legality of it all. But I think it's definitely coming to a rise with people like the New York Times coming out and suing OpenAI, and that's going to be hitting the courts and seeing what is resolved from that. I think that is going to start playing out.

Yeah, you're right. Some people that have arguments against AI can't really point to a specific penal code and be like, well, they're breaking this law right here. Are they using fair use wrongly due to this reasoning? I think a lot of arguments that they have will become more resolved in the next five to 10 years as court systems resolve some of these issues. Who knows, maybe even in five to 10 years there's a new tool or a new model that is using some type of new technology that arises new moral issues that they're going to have to fight against. It's almost like this issue that the technology is moving faster than the courts could ever move to resolve any of this debate, which is a big issue.

But at least to me, I think it always comes down to the way that the tool is being used. A lot of the debate is with regards to visual art and visual artists, but OpenAI is a lot more, and a lot of these AI models are a lot more than just text to image. It's text to text. So we have authors and writers being scraped and their copyrighted work being plagiarized to some degree, and programmers being plagiarized with their code being scraped. And anybody can be a coder now. Anybody can be an artist now. Anybody can be a writer now is the term.

And I think there's definitely arguments on both sides that I can agree with, but it's always tough to see what exactly is correct. But at least to me, it's always coming down to a determinant factor of how it's being used. And we see a lot of what the Christie's AI auction with artists being berated by people online, and maybe they aren't always berating the right people, because sometimes these artists that you're berating are artists that aren't even using these black boxed corporate models. They're actually training their own. So the complexity of the technology that you mentioned, Peter, you really have to dive into it to understand it, to understand the ways people are using it, to make a better, I think, informed decision on what you think is right and wrong. But yeah, I think that's what it's always going to come down to for me, is how it's being used.

thefunnyguys: Yeah, I want to totally echo what you say there, Conrad. I think a lot of the criticism talks about AI art, but it doesn't necessarily acknowledge all the nuances within the AI art category. Sure, some artists, they may be using these large text-to-image models, and maybe in their prompts they are referencing existing artists. That might be happening. We don't know for sure. But I think specifically with this Christie's auction, the curation was actually done really well. I would say most of the artists, if not all of them, they use their own training data, they train their own models. There are no artists being ripped off by the artists in the Christie's auction, as far as I'm concerned.

There is a larger societal issue where big tech or companies like OpenAI reap all the benefits from generative AI and there's no value being redistributed to the creators of the training data. I think that is just a fact. And it would be really interesting to see these big companies at least try to redistribute some of the value, because they all talk about AGI and how AI will be able to do anything for humans and human labor as it exists today and knowledge work will be a thing of the past. But to get people excited by this future, I think you also need to paint a picture of how humans will still manage to survive. At the moment, none of that is being done by big tech.

But I do think there's some really interesting experiments that are being done by artists. Earlier this quarter I went to The Call by Holly Herndon and Mat Dryhurst. And there was some super interesting discussions between lawyers, between the curator, between someone from the company of Holly and Mat, Spawning, where they discussed a number of experiments to redistribute some of this created value to the creators of the original training data. Art can really be a fantastic playground for these new models of social coordination. In an artistic practice you can show it as a one-off. You can try to go from zero to one and create this... The way they did it was create this data trust that basically aggregates the rights. If someone wants to use that training data, value would be redistributed to this collective. I think what they were doing is really fascinating. They try it out on a one-off basis. If it works, if it has potential, they can try to scale it through the company, Spawning.ai.

To me it's interesting that Mat Dryhurst is being attacked by some of these people, while he's one of the very few in the world who is actually trying to create new social coordination mechanisms. We need more of these experiments. A lot of the critique doesn't necessarily come forward with alternatives for social coordination.

Peter Bauman: Yeah, I think what both of you bring up is that equating generative AI with only these large commercial models is just an oversimplification. And there are things going back to VAEs, variational autoencoders and GANs. More than 10 years ago, artists started using these deep generative models that had, again, nothing to do with Silicon Valley, nothing to do with pressing a button and plagiarism. These were all bespokenly trained models.

And then also, Conrad, I think what you were talking about, artists are not only using text to image. I think that's a really big point, that this is coming for everything. It's text to image, it's text to text, it's text to video, it's text to audio. Because of that, Le Random has been pulled into that, because our content has been scraped. We can say with some degree of likelihood, I think, that our content has been scraped. We know how it feels. It doesn't always feel right to have that done without having any say, and that it just happens and you can't really stop it. Yeah, it doesn't feel right. We definitely understand that having your work scraped in a non-consensual way feels invasive and it feels wrong. It can feel morally wrong. We understand that perspective literally from a first-hand stance.

That's why it's important to think about this more from a place of moving forward. That's what Jan talked about, and people that we really respect in this space, like Mat Dryhurst. What are the actual solutions? How can we actually fix this? Is that going to be some compensation model? Is that going to be some opt-out framework? What are the actual steps that can be taken, as opposed to just saying we cannot and will not use it? I don't know. I think that would be, in 1995, saying, okay, we are never going to use the internet, or in 1965 saying, I'm never going to use a computer. It might not just be possible in the future. It's hard to say. I think a more practical stance is thinking about not just shutting them off, therefore also not realizing any of their benefits, but thinking about how to most ethically and morally work with them moving forward.

Conrad House: Yeah, I think you're completely right. People have the right to feel angry at this non-consensual scraping of their work. It doesn't just hurt when your work is getting scraped. It hurts even more when that scraped data is being used to then have somebody else create some product that they are in some ways claiming as their own, when in reality the basis of that work is yours.

It's interesting to see, or it's pretty telling to see, OpenAI's response to this happening to themselves, when back in November there was the group of AI artists that were invited to work with OpenAI when Sora and newer models came out. In a way they fought back with their manifesto that was entitled "Art in the Cage of Digital Reproduction," where they took this new private model that they had access to with OpenAI and they publicized it. They open-sourced it to Hugging Face and they allowed anybody to come in and start using this model. We saw how fast OpenAI was to attack that and get that taken off the internet and have no access to it anymore. It's in a way almost hypocritical of them to be like, well, we can play by our own rules, and when you try to follow the same rules that we're following, we're going to attack you for it and we're going to take it down, because that just really doesn't make much sense.

I think it also goes to show the power that OpenAI has to be able to enforce these type of restrictions on this technology. If only artists themselves could also, or writers themselves could also, enforce that same type of practicality of taking power in your own work and going to maybe OpenAI and being like, hey, don't scrape Le Random. Having the power to do that, the same power as OpenAI had to go to Hugging Face and be like, hey, take this model off. You don't have rights to this.

I think this goes back to when we talk about the legality issues of this all. It's like, even when these do hit the court or when these do hit maybe political realms, who is going to be lobbying the politicians to decide on what is right and what is wrong? OpenAI has such a huge amount of capital that they could really influence in a lot of ways and probably pave a path that's going to be best for them. The smaller guys that are getting scraped and exploited aren't going to have a say in it all. And I think that's what makes it a bit more scary too, to some degree, and really just trying to find the best path to do this in the morally best way is a very tricky avenue.

Peter Bauman: Yeah, I think it's important to separate the broader technology like the internet or deep learning with some of the bad actors who might use or leverage that technology for maybe sometimes positive events, but also sometimes negative events, like OpenAI. Yeah, there's obviously lots of issues. I mean, there's been a mass exodus of employees. There's been an employee letter that was signed by hundreds of OpenAI employees, including Alec Radford, who we've written about. So we are certainly not advocating for this work to not be critically examined, but to just lump it all together is lazy.

thefunnyguys: I think what makes it so difficult, also for creators, to take a stance on this is that AI is so polyvalent. It can do so many things. Sure, it can maybe recreate art or images in your style as an artist. But at the same time, it might also help a collector or a visitor to a museum to take a picture of your work and recognize that it's yours. For example, for you, Peter, when you write an article, AI can also distribute your content and it can acknowledge that you are the creator of this article. Yeah, that's, I think, also the issue that some creators have to deal with. Yes, there's some cons, but there's also pros, and which ones outweigh others. It's not always easy to determine.

And there are some writers, like Tyler Cowen, the economist, who explicitly says that he is writing for the machines. He wants LLMs to train on his work. He wants to be very present in these networks. He wants these ideas to be redirected to him as a person. And I think he's afraid that if he doesn't do that, that he will be to some extent forgotten. He wants his name to show up in the ChatGPT responses. Yeah, I wonder, Peter, for you, as a writer, how do you think about that? Do you also want to be in the training data for these LLMs, or do you prefer to not be scraped?

Peter Bauman: I think that's that important issue of consent. It's important just to be part of the conversation and to be asked. I don't think it's that difficult to envision a scenario in the future where there's optimization, there's SEO for these LLMs and for getting your content higher in terms of the neural network and optimizing for promoting your voice and promoting your influence in the algorithm. So, yeah, I certainly think that that is coming.

And the overall broad point is that the cat is out of the bag to a certain extent. I think we can all agree on that. And so it's more about shaping the future direction of that ball rolling down the hill, or that, I don't know, the cat outside of the bag or whatever, than putting it back in. It's a more practical standpoint to begin the conversation at than cutting it off and never using it, because there might be any number of reasons why that could backfire.

But one area that AI maybe did fall back on, and it helps to point these out too, because this isn't just continual up only. Everything is always just getting better and better every day. But there are some things that have fallen off a bit in AI, and one of those trends is in AI agents. I know that this quarter especially, it seemed like at the beginning of last year they were really gaining and rising in popularity. And then that seems to have crashed this quarter. Or what we've at the very least learned is that they're not ready. What do you guys think about these generative AI agents and their penchant for things like just giving wrong information? Is it that they died this quarter, or is it just that they weren't ready yet?

Conrad House: I don't know if they've died or if they're not ready yet, but I do agree that they are... At least everyone that I've seen has been very low quality. I mean, it comes down to just pure large language model slop that they're producing to some degree nowadays, and misinformation directly, where sometimes you have these market bots that are tweeting these recaps of things, and you look deeper into the actual market data instead of just taking the tweet as 100 percent factual, and you realize, well, how are they even tweeting this? This never happened. This sale never happened. This project never saw this much volume. How is it getting these figures? It makes it really tough to even become trusting of them.

On top of that, at the very surface level, they aren't really providing any additional dialog within the space that's actually beneficial and hasn't been talked about for months or even years already in the space. I think one reference to it is the fxhash price discussion channel, or fxchat, is a better, I think, indicator of market than an AI bot could ever do, because it's just going to spew the same top-of-the-line talking points or top-of-the-line artists that everyone already knows about. And this idea that you could have an AI agent that could do really deep research for you is really enticing. Having something that's super efficient with recognizing data points or recognizing emerging artists or whatever it may be. At this point it seems like we're sacrificing quality for this efficiency, and we're sacrificing a lot of quality in a lot of ways.

And it's also just this idea that these AI agents or even autonomous artists are facades for really poor tech or really poor token hype. They aren't really even in it for the technology. They're in it to pretend to be something that they're not in a lot of ways. And it's a big question that's been brought up, especially around the Botto auction that happens, but not just with Botto, but with all these other autonomous artists, which is really, what is the degree of autonomy with these agents? There's always going to be the analogy of a man behind the curtain that's controlling these levers and pedals and really guiding these agents in a way.

Flynn, for example, was this autonomous artist that was accepted into a university arts program. But what does that even entail? Is this bot agent going to sit in on these university Zoom calls and classes? Then is it going to, after that class, take notes and study those notes and then sign into some university online whiteboard where it has assignments that it has to finish, and it's able to take a final exam? All of that doesn't seem doable in the infrastructure of agents that we have. It still seems like at the end of the day Flynn is going to have to have some human controlling it and guiding it, or maybe uploading an assignment to a ChatGPT thing and asking for the response to that assignment, or giving it some prompt to do some type of artistic project that it has to do.

To me it all seems like what I said before, a big facade to really poor tech, or sometimes even just used to induce a token hype that they can release and create some revenue on some DEXs with it. And it's this idea that the attention spans of the space that we're in are short and everyone is just trying to grasp for the next big thing. Everyone is trying to grasp for the next thing that they can make a few bucks on and not really looking back on, well, what is this actually doing? Is this actually beneficial to what we're trying to create or trying to push forward in the space?

thefunnyguys: Yeah, I'll take the other side of the discussion here. I do agree with you guys. The social agents, the agents that are basically connected to Twitter accounts, they're quite annoying. They're not factually correct. They make way too many mistakes for us to trust them in any regard. I also think a lot of the AI artists being autonomous, I also think that narrative was not actually correct. It was way too early to really claim, in my opinion, that this artist is fully autonomous.

But I do think there are a lot of interesting AI agent applications that do already create value. There's these functional AI agents. For example, all the deep research tools like OpenAI's or Gemini's. I think these are already super useful. They crawl the web, they find information on so many different sources and they aggregate it really nicely in a very insightful way. And even preparing for this podcast, I did ask some of these research tools to summarize the main happenings in digital art in the first quarter of 2025. And I would say maybe half of it was actually interesting. The other half was, I would say, maybe some noise that it picked up on from the internet that wasn't really insightful. But still, it saved me a lot of time. It did bring some interesting talking points forward.

And there's also this company called Sierra AI, which is being helmed by Bret Taylor, the chairman of the board at OpenAI. And they create agents for companies, specifically agents to help with customer service. And I think that's definitely going to be really big. Bret says himself that in 1995 every company needed some type of website strategy. And he believes that now every company needs some type of agent strategy just to assist customers without necessarily requiring human capital. I think that's already quite interesting as of today. That will only get better in the future.

And maybe as a final point, I think agents are also interesting in the context of DAOs. When Vitalik coined the term DAO, I think from the start he talked about automation being at the center and humans being at the edges. But I believe in 2015 that was not really possible. There were still a lot of humans involved, even at the center of the DAO. But now with AI agents, it might actually be possible to automate the center of the DAO to some extent, but still have the humans in charge of the DAO.

And there's one really interesting experiment called Aiden that was launched by Tribute Labs, I think one or two months ago, where basically humans submit projects, like new companies, like new startups that the DAO could potentially invest in. All of this information is then being analyzed by a swarm of agents. And then all of these agents, they also vote on the proposal. And every agent votes from a different perspective. Like one of them may be a marketing expert, another one may be more focused on the financials, or maybe a value investor. But then all of these votes of all these different agents get aggregated for the DAO members. They can use all of this input to then decide, are we actually going to invest in this project or not? And to me it's super interesting. These orchestration layers will only get better over time as the models improve. And as long as the orchestration is there, the models just need to be updated, basically, for the product to become better. I'm actually quite excited about agents, but agreed. At the moment there's a lot of slop.

Peter Bauman: I think your point highlights that integration with protocol art and deep learning systems. And again, it's such a compelling use case for creativity that it's hard to see it going away, or ignoring it being really the solution.

Maybe we can go to that third broad topic that we as a team together wanted to discuss regarding the first quarter of 2025. And we touched on a lot of these things, the negative connotations with AI. A lot of those similar things can be said about NFTs. NFTs was the original scam, the insta-scam, and AI in a lot of ways has taken on the mantle. I'm wondering, we've seen through various moments in 2025 this relationship between NFTs and digital art challenged a bit. And this goes back to this unfinished article that I hope I finish someday called "The Three Body Problem for Art," that is based on Sam Hart's "Three Body Problem for Crypto," which basically just refers to this unstable relationship between technology and markets and crypto due to the lack of regulation. And so I just extend that to the art field.

And it talks about some of the benefits of NFTs. They offer ownership and provenance and autonomy and things like that, but they can also be entangled in speculation and hype. And so focusing on NFTs in general may detract from more meaningful artistic explorations of digital media and networked culture. And so ultimately that piece advocates for more of a stance of integration with institutions rather than this NFT exceptionalism and NFT separatism. And so, yeah, I just wonder what you guys think about that. I think, if anything, this quarter has offered a lot of interesting data points for how you feel about that one way or the other.

thefunnyguys: How I think about it at the moment is that it should definitely never be the start of a conversation. You shouldn't introduce yourself as an NFT artist, or if you're a curator you shouldn't curate a show of NFTs. I think that really typically creates a barrier between the listener or the spectator and the artist or the curator, because people still have a lot of negative connotations to the word NFT. Most people in society, when they think of the word NFT, they think of 2021, when cartoon monkeys were going for millions of dollars.

But as an artist, if you start by introducing your practice by talking about the art and the message, maybe by showing the visual works you're creating, then I do think that if the listener is still interested and you're having a good conversation, you shouldn't shy away from using the word NFT necessarily. Because in the end, if someone is really interested and they want to potentially acquire the work, they need to know it's an NFT. It comes with certain difficulties. They will have to create a crypto wallet. They might have to buy some cryptocurrency. They need to protect their crypto wallet. It's important to acknowledge that it is an NFT in the end, I think. And maybe right now, because there's not much speculation going on, there's not many PFP projects being successful, maybe it's also a good moment to try to reclaim the word to some extent and try to create some positive connotations. But yeah, I'm curious what you guys think about it.

Conrad House: Yeah, I think in general it's still something that... It's a term, at least the term NFT, is something I still try to distance myself from. A direct storyline is whenever we talk to artists that are not within the NFT space, and we're maybe trying to commission work from them that we want tokenized on the blockchain, there's always this split second hesitation or self cringe when I have to bring up the term NFT. So there's a lot of ways you try to avoid it and just maybe refer to it as tokenized art. We're trying to tokenize the art in some ways, because there is a stigma to it.

And I think my distancing from that term is not just from the stigma standpoint, but also I think to some degree that it just doesn't always make sense. I think Dan and Yosi brought this up in a Metaversal podcast recently that I really liked. But the NFT is just the vehicle at which the medium is being presented and shown and transferred in a way. And you wouldn't apply that same concept to other medias. If I wanted to recommend a song or an album to Peter, I wouldn't be like, hey, go listen to this MP3, it's really fantastic. Or if I wanted to show you an image, I wouldn't say, hey, look at this awesome JPEG that I saw. Or even a painting, I wouldn't go to Jan and be like, hey, look at this awesome linen canvas that I saw. It just doesn't make sense when the NFT really isn't a core part of the work. It's just the vehicle at which the work is being presented, or at least transferred within the infrastructure that it lives.

Trying to create a term that better describes the piece of media that you're working with, whether that's, oh, it's a digital tokenized art, and not reducing it down to something that's as simple as NFTs, because even work that we see within the space can't be reduced to that term of just an NFT. It's the idea that the contract is the art sometimes, and the contract is not the art piece in and of itself. It's a contract. It's a blockchain tool that you're using. For example, we talk about maybe like PXLDEX or Infinite Garden by Leander Herzog, where the contract is a tool and the NFTs that are coming from this contract are a part of the greater art piece. It's not the art piece in and of itself. So I think trying to maybe think of a better way of not over-focusing on the tech aspect of it and just calling digital art for what it is. And that's art at the end of the day.

Peter Bauman: Yeah, exactly. I think that wraps up my quarter one takeaways of where my thought has developed on this. My sense is more that I don't feel the need to use the term very much. It feels mostly perfunctory. If you're in the space, you know their uses and their benefits and how easy it is to collect. They can still be interesting on a conceptual level, things like art that take advantage of the certain unique characteristics of Ethereum or blockchains, and work that engages with broader aesthetics or social or political questions that use the blockchain. That is great.

If you're bringing up blockchain, typically how I see it is when it's brought up as a proxy for the market or sales. When that becomes what anybody, and it doesn't even have to be artists, just thought leaders or whatever in the space, tweet about NFTs a lot. I wish they would just move on and talk about something else. Which, hey, maybe that is also what we should do.

thefunnyguys: I do think one issue with using the word NFT too much is also that maybe people will think that when an artist uses blockchain technology, that is the only thing they do. They use an NFT to sell one visual image. With many artists who use blockchain technology, that's not the case. We're going to talk about it later, but PXLDEX by Kim Asendorf, or Cycles by Material Protocol Arts, or Terraforms. If you would just say this artist is creating NFTs, it would only touch maybe 10 percent of the entire project, and you would lose so much conceptual depth by just reducing it to NFTs. So maybe in general it's just better as an artist to say that you use blockchain technology, not necessarily reducing it to NFTs. The term blockchain technology might also have less negative connotations. It might be less of a conversation killer.

Peter Bauman: Yeah, it reminds me of something that William Mapan recently said to Leila at Verse. Basically he brings up first that he's a multidisciplinary artist and emphasizes color. Then maybe the very last thing he says is that maybe if they're interested in purchasing the work, even that is when he might mention the NFT. But other than that it's basically perfunctory. I think that is a healthy way to think about it at the end of the first quarter in 2025.

One really interesting example is this exhibition at the Toledo Museum of Art called Infinite Images: The Art of Algorithms, and it is including some artists who we don't traditionally associate with algorithms. What do you guys think about this really interesting, I think, showcase of artists who typically work with NFTs in an institutional setting?

thefunnyguys: Yeah, it's definitely a very interesting choice for Sam Spratt. First of all, it was really fantastic to see how many collectors, how many spectators deeply connected with Sam's new body of work. I think it was so far in this year definitely one of the big successes, one of the projects that got the most attention. And a lot of people seem to have found deep meaning in the project. And I guess as an artist that's all you can really wish for.

But it was quite surprising, to say the least, to see Sam Spratt being curated in this exhibition, because the title of the exhibition is literally Infinite Images: The Art of Algorithms. It's really about algorithms. A lot of the other artists that will be part of the exhibition, like Operator or Sofia Crespo, Vera Molnár, all of them have a very intimate connection with algorithms. They've been using them for a very long time. It's integral to their practice. It's how they express themselves as an artist. They create algorithms.

When Sam speaks, when he talks about this project, I think he really deemphasizes the use of algorithms. He literally says that the project is not... There's no randomness in the project. It's not about algorithms, it's about human connection. Then I do find it quite strange, from a curatorial perspective, to put his art in an exhibition solely dedicated to algorithms, because there's so many artists, hundreds, if not thousands, that have been creating interesting work with algorithms. All of them could have had this spot in this exhibition. But for some reason the curator did land on Sam Spratt. I'm really curious to see why they decided to curate Sam Spratt into the show.

Conrad House: Yeah, I agree. The curatorial vision may... It seems at least a bit confusing, or maybe even a bit misaligned, to include Spratt in that exhibition. But I think a lot of this can mirror what we see in the traditional art world. And at least it's something that's, I think, a bit humorous to me is when NFTs or this entire digital art on the blockchain started taking off, one of the big positive components that everyone kept reiterating was that we can build a new landscape for art. We can build a new landscape in which artists are represented and showcased in a lot of ways. It was really exciting that we can break out of these traditional barriers and traditional rules.

thefunnyguys: I think, Peter, you're being quite humble by leaving out that in 2025 you've been appointed to be a juror for the SIGGRAPH Distinguished Artist Awards. I actually think that's quite big. Huge congrats on joining the jury. This award has been around for decades. It celebrates the most impactful digital artists. And there's only a few jury members, right? It's you and a handful of other people. Five people in total. So, yeah, huge congrats. It's really awesome to have you as part of the jury.

Peter Bauman: Thank you. Yeah, I was not expecting that at all, to be invited to be on it, but it's a really big honor to lend my voice to that selection process. And so, yeah, actually that is going to be happening soon. And so we'll be selecting the 2025 winner soon, and that will be announced soon. And then I'll be on the jury next year for 2026 too. Really exciting, really fun, really humbling to be part of it. It was such an interesting group of people too. Yeah, and really exciting to see who has been nominated, and I'm looking forward to seeing who wins. But yeah, well, thanks, guys. I mean, great chat. It was really fun to go over all this.

Conrad House: Thanks, everybody, for having this talk. And thanks for anybody that's listening in and stuck with us throughout this entire time.

thefunnyguys: Yeah, definitely. Thank you, Peter. Thank you, Conrad. This was fun. And, yeah, thanks to the listeners.
